::: {.lead}
Today you make the website of Mona's Cakes, the service of Lecture 8. Each
experiment has two parts. **Part A** is in Google Sites (a free website
builder) or in Notepad. **Part B** is on a simulator of the interactive
lesson: on paper, scan its QR code; on the screen, click its link. After
each step, write your result in its box. At the end, copy your key results
into the table.
:::

## Before you start

- **You need:** a lab computer with a browser and a Google account (Google
  Sites at `sites.google.com`), and Notepad for Experiment 3.
- **No lab computer today?** Do Part B of each experiment on your phone.
- **Check:** the results are at the end of this worksheet. Look only after
  you try. On the interactive lesson, every step has a check that answers
  at once.

{{< start-files >}}

## Experiment 1 · The plan and the pages

**The idea:** plan a website first: its **purpose** (to take orders), its
**audience** (families) and its **pages**. A small service needs three
pages: **Home** (who you are), **Service** (what you offer, with the order
button) and **Contact** (how to reach you). A **website builder** such as
Google Sites makes the pages without code; the **menu** (navigation)
joins them.

**Aim:** plan the pages, and build them in Google Sites.

::: {.part}
**Part A · In the app (Google Sites)**
:::

1. Open `sites.google.com` and click **Blank site** (+). Type the site
   name `Mona's Cakes` and the page title `Cakes made at home`.

   {{< record "The first page of the site is called" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Home**: every new site starts with its home page.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   Which page says who you are and what you offer?

   - [x] Home

     Why: The home page is the first page that visitors see.

   - [ ] Contact

     Why: Contact says how to reach you.

   - [ ] Service

     Why: Service gives the details of what you offer.
   :::

2. Open **Pages** (on the right) and click **+**: add the pages `Service`
   and `Contact`.

   {{< record "The menu at the top shows … pages" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **3 pages**: Home, Service and Contact. The menu (navigation) shows
   them at the top of every page.
   :::

   ::: {.fill answer="3|three" unit="pages" hint="Home, then the two new pages."}
   Mona's site has Home, Service and Contact. How many pages does its menu
   show?

   Why: Three pages, one link for each in the menu.
   :::

::: {.part}
**Part B · On the simulator** (no computer? do it on your phone)
:::

{{< sim file="sims/site-planner.html" poster="sims/site-planner.png" title="Site Planner: what goes on which page?" >}}

3. In **Site Planner**, put the six parts of the content on the right
   pages. On which page is the button *Order now*?

   {{< record "Order now is on" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   The **Service** page: the customer sees the cakes and orders there.
   :::

   ::: {.sort}
   Which page? Sort the content.

   Home
   :   Welcome to Mona's Cakes! Cakes made at home.

       Why: The home page says who you are.

   Service
   :   The cakes and their prices.

       Why: What the customer can get.

   :   The button Order now.

       Why: The customer orders on the service page.

   Contact
   :   The phone number and the address.

       Why: How to reach you.
   :::

## Experiment 2 · The design and the phone view

**The idea:** a good design is easy to read: one **theme** (the same
colours and fonts on every page), **strong contrast** (dark text on light),
pictures of a good size, and a clear **menu**. Most visitors use a phone:
check the **mobile view** before you publish (Preview › the phone).

**Aim:** give the site one look, and check it on a phone.

::: {.part}
**Part A · In the app (Google Sites)**
:::

1. Open **Themes** (on the right) and choose a theme. On the Home page,
   **Insert › Images** and add a picture (Search or Upload).

   {{< record "The name of my theme" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   For example **Simple**, **Aristotle** or **Diplomat**. The theme gives
   all pages the same colours and fonts.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   Why use one theme for the whole site?

   - [x] Every page gets the same colours and fonts.

     Why: The site looks clear and the same on every page.

   - [ ] It adds more pages.

     Why: A theme changes the look, not the pages.

   - [ ] It publishes the site.

     Why: Publish is a separate button.
   :::

2. Click **Preview** (the eye) and choose the **phone**. Look at the menu.

   {{< record "On the phone, the menu is" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   A small button with three lines (**≡**): the menu opens when you tap it.
   The page is narrow, so short text and big buttons help.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   On a phone, how does the menu of the site look?

   - [x] a button with three lines (≡)

     Why: A narrow screen has no room for all the links.

   - [ ] it is not there

     Why: It is still there, behind the ≡ button.

   - [ ] very small links in one long line

     Why: The site makes a ≡ button instead.
   :::

::: {.part}
**Part B · On the simulator** (no computer? do it on your phone)
:::

{{< sim file="sims/design-check.html" poster="sims/design-check.png" title="Design Check: fix the page" >}}

3. In **Design Check**, fix the four problems of the page, then press
   **Preview: phone**. Which problem made the text hard to read?

   {{< record "The problem of the text (one word)" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **The contrast**: light grey text on white. Dark text on a light
   background is easy to read.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   Light grey text on a white page. What is the problem?

   - [x] weak contrast

     Why: Use dark text on a light background.

   - [ ] too many pages

     Why: The number of pages does not change how the text looks.

   - [ ] no picture

     Why: A picture does not make the text easier to read.
   :::

## Experiment 3 · A look at HTML and CSS

**The idea:** behind every web page is **HTML**, the content, written with
**tags**: `<h1>` a big heading, `<p>` a paragraph, `<a href="…">` a link,
`<img>` a picture. **CSS** sets the look: `h1 { color: brown; }`. Google
Sites writes them for you; here you only look and change one word.

**Aim:** read a tiny web page, and change its look with CSS.

::: {.part}
**Part A · In the app (Notepad and a browser)**
:::

1. Open `page-start.html` in a browser. Then open it in **Notepad**
   (right-click › Open with › Notepad). Find the line with `<h1>`.

   {{< record "The text of the heading h1" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Mona's Cakes**: the big heading of the page.
   :::

   ::: {.sort}
   What does each tag make? Sort them.

   a heading
   :   `<h1>`

       Why: h1 is the biggest heading.

   a paragraph
   :   `<p>`

       Why: p is a paragraph of text.

   a link
   :   `<a href="…">`

       Why: a goes to another page.
   :::

2. In Notepad, change `color: brown` to `color: green`. Save (Ctrl + S),
   then refresh the browser (F5).

   {{< record "The heading is now" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Green**. You changed the CSS: the look changed, the text stayed the
   same.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   You changed `color: brown` to `color: green`. What changed on the page?

   - [x] only the colour of the heading

     Why: CSS changes the look, not the text.

   - [ ] the text of the heading

     Why: The text is in the HTML, and it did not change.

   - [ ] the link

     Why: The CSS line is for h1, the heading.
   :::

::: {.part}
**Part B · On the simulator** (no computer? do it on your phone)
:::

{{< sim file="sims/html-lab.html" poster="sims/html-lab.png" title="HTML Lab: a look at HTML and CSS" >}}

3. In **HTML Lab**, change the colour and the size of the heading, and
   answer the three questions. Which tag makes a link?

   {{< record "A link is the tag" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **`<a>`** with `href`: the address of the page that it opens.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   Which language sets the colour of the heading?

   - [x] CSS

     Why: CSS sets colours, fonts and sizes.

   - [ ] HTML

     Why: HTML says what is on the page.

   - [ ] Excel

     Why: Excel is for sheets of data.
   :::
